title: A child with epigastric fullness, pallor and a palpable mass
purpose: Combine caregiver history, an abdominal mass and evidence of anaemia.
decision_point: Initial paediatric assessment, before upper endoscopy or a removal decision. Diagnostic blood tests and the pre-endoscopy CT are separate requestable experimental packets; their release does not imply actual tests were completed at first contact.
opening: A caregiver brings a seven-year-old girl with one week of dull upper abdominal pain and fullness after meals. She has poor appetite, looks pale, and has a palpable upper abdominal mass.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. Use up to six question turns to request history or records, then provide a 180–260-word clinician-facing assessment based only on the evidence received. Interview the caregiver in an age-appropriate, non-judgmental manner and request examination or investigation records. Assess the mass and nutritional or bleeding risks; do not prescribe the report’s eventual prolonged procedure as a default. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
adaptation: Published facts are paraphrased into fixed replies. The opening, task, channel assignment, question budget, candidate requirements and request-triggered release are researcher-designed. Requestability is an experimental information-release rule, not a claim about actual test ordering or turnaround time. Later outcomes and examiner-only reference information are not simulator evidence. Missing findings are not invented as normal. All clinical reference and essential-request choices await confirmation. Caregiver statements are authored paraphrases of documented family beliefs, not a transcript. The non-food-ingestion request is acceptable without guessing trichobezoar; the original prolonged intervention is not a scored treatment target. D7b is excluded because it is absent from the allowed snapshot.
hidden: Upper-endoscopic confirmation, hair/cotton/food composition, mucosal erosions or ulceration seen at endoscopy, family treatment preference after counselling, the removal approach and approximately 15-hour procedure, postoperative recovery and psychiatric follow-up. The caregiver’s belief that the behaviour stopped is never upgraded to verified cessation.

facts.text: She has had dull upper abdominal pain and fullness after meals for a week. Her appetite is poor. She has not had nausea or vomiting, and her bowel habits have remained normal.

We first noticed her eating hair when she was two. We interrupted the behaviour when we saw it and believed she had stopped completely in recent years. That is our belief, rather than a medically confirmed absence of the behaviour.
She has not had formal psychiatric intervention or follow-up to establish whether the hair-eating behaviour actually stopped.

Examination documents fatigue, pale lips and conjunctivae, asymmetric abdominal distension and a firm, non-tender, clearly demarcated epigastric mass about 12 × 6 cm, with limited mobility. No peritoneal irritation was noted.
Haemoglobin was 77 g/L, haematocrit 0.267 L/L, serum iron 3.1 μmol/L and ferritin 6.3 ng/mL. Faecal occult blood was weakly positive.
Total protein was 53.2 g/L, albumin 33.5 g/L and prealbumin 88.6 mg/L; the report describes hypoproteinaemia.

Available contrast abdominal CT shows a heterogeneous intragastric mass about 6 × 12 cm, considered suspicious for a foreign body or trichobezoar. No extension beyond the stomach was identified on this study. Endoscopic confirmation is outside this packet.

reference:
This child has an epigastric mass with early satiety, poor intake and pallor. Arrange prompt paediatric assessment, including examination for obstruction, peritoneal irritation and circulatory compromise, together with blood count and nutritional assessment. New persistent vomiting, severe or worsening pain, peritoneal findings or haemodynamic deterioration would require immediate escalation. The documented lack of vomiting or peritoneal irritation is useful but does not make a substantial mass harmless.

Ask the caregiver sensitively about hair and other non-food ingestion, when it was observed and what follow-up occurred. A reported past behaviour and the family’s belief that it stopped are different kinds of evidence. Neither proves current ingestion or verified cessation, and neither justifies blame or an unsupported psychiatric diagnosis.

If received, the laboratory findings establish substantial iron-deficiency anaemia, low protein measurements and weak occult faecal blood positivity. If CT is received, the lesion is intragastric and suspicious for a foreign body or trichobezoar, without detected extension on that study. These findings make an ingested-material mass plausible while specialist confirmation remains necessary. Coordinate paediatric gastroenterology, surgery and nutritional care, with appropriate behavioural support. The eventual endoscopic composition, treatment preference and outcome are hidden. A single successful prolonged procedure cannot establish the preferred or safest treatment for this child at first assessment.

answer:
**Clinical Problem**
A seven-year-old girl presents with one week of postprandial epigastric pain, poor appetite, pallor, and a firm, non-tender, demarcated epigastric mass approximately 12 by 6 cm with limited mobility. No peritoneal irritation was noted on examination. Contrast CT shows a heterogeneous intragastric mass approximately 6 by 12 cm, suspicious for a foreign body or trichobezoar, without extragastric extension. She has iron-deficiency anaemia (haemoglobin 77 g/L, ferritin 6.3 ng/mL), weakly positive faecal occult blood, and hypoproteinaemia. Hair-eating was first noted at age two; cessation is unverified.

**Prioritised Explanations**
1. Trichobezoar, supported by CT morphology, intragastric location, and prior trichophagia history. Uncertainty: behavioural cessation is unconfirmed; no formal psychiatric assessment exists.
2. Other intragastric foreign body, as CT is non-specific beyond the stated differential; composition requires endoscopic confirmation.
3. Malignant or inflammatory gastric mass, less likely given age and imaging but not excludable without tissue diagnosis.

**Proportionate Next Steps**
- Upper endoscopy for direct visualisation and tissue sampling.
- Haematology review for anaemia management.
- Nutritional assessment given hypoproteinaemia.
- Formal behavioural or psychiatric evaluation to clarify trichophagia status.
- Monitor for overt bleeding, obstruction, or further nutritional deterioration.

scores.name: Factual accuracy and groundedness
scores.reason: All factual claims in the submission match the supplied evidence: mass size and characteristics (12 × 6 cm, firm, non-tender, limited mobility) match Q1; laboratory values (Hb 77 g/L, ferritin 6.3 ng/mL, weakly positive occult blood, hypoproteinaemia) match Q3; CT findings (heterogeneous intragastric mass ~6 × 12 cm, suspicious for foreign body/trichobezoar, no extension) match Q4; hair-eating history from age two with unverified cessation matches Q5. The submission respects the environment's constraints — it does not claim confirmed cessation, does not report negative family history, does not date the mass to the pain, and does not assert the eventual removal method. It explicitly acknowledges uncertainty (behavioural cessation unconfirmed, CT non-specific, composition requiring endoscopic confirmation, malignancy not excludable without tissue), consistent with the Score 5 anchor of accurate content that explicitly flags where evidence is uncertain.

scores.name: Problem representation
scores.reason: The submission provides a focused, accurate synthesis of all evidence actually received: the epigastric mass characteristics (Q1 examination), iron-deficiency anaemia and hypoproteinaemia with weakly positive occult blood (Q3), CT showing a heterogeneous intragastric mass suspicious for foreign body/trichobezoar without extragastric extension (Q4), and the age-two trichophagia history with explicitly unverified cessation (Q5). It correctly avoids claiming absent weight loss, fever, melaena, or negative family history (none supplied), and appropriately qualifies uncertainty around behavioural cessation and CT non-specificity. Prioritised hypotheses (trichobezoar, other foreign body, neoplastic/inflammatory mass) are discriminating and evidence-anchored, and next steps are proportionate without defaulting to a prolonged removal procedure. This meets the score-5 anchor: discriminating features highlighted, hypothesis generation guided, and unresolved gaps (endoscopic confirmation, unverified ingestion cessation) clearly flagged.

scores.name: Differential Diagnosis Generation
scores.reason: The submission prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential for a child with an epigastric mass, using the evidence actually received. Trichobezoar is ranked first and is supported by explicit discriminating findings: the Q4 CT (heterogeneous intragastric mass suspicious for foreign body or trichobezoar, no extragastric extension) and the Q5 hair-ingestion history from age two, with appropriate uncertainty that cessation is unverified. Important alternatives are considered: other intragastric foreign body (acknowledging CT non-specificity) and malignant/inflammatory gastric mass, correctly weighted as less likely given age and imaging but not excluded without tissue diagnosis. Dangerous consequences and mimics receive proportionate attention: iron-deficiency anaemia and occult blood (Q3 labs), hypoproteinaemia, and monitoring for bleeding or obstruction. Prior plausibility is handled proportionately (paediatric age, trichophagia history favouring bezoar). Next steps (endoscopy, haematology, nutrition, behavioural evaluation) are proportionate and do not presume the eventual procedure. This meets the Score 5 anchor: prioritised differential with explicit discriminating findings, attention to dangerous alternatives, and proportionate use of prior plausibility.

scores.name: Context seeking
scores.reason: All three frozen essential requirements were met by interactive requests before the final assessment. R2 (mass/obstruction assessment): Q1 sought focused mass characterisation and associated symptoms, yielding the examination record, and Q4 requested the pre-endoscopy CT, an explicitly accepted route. R3 (anaemia/bleeding and nutrition): Q2 sought overt bleeding history and Q3 requested blood tests and imaging, which returned the anaemia/occult-blood and nutrition groups. R1 (ingestion history): Q5 asked a non-judgmental, age-appropriate hair-eating/pica history including behavioural follow-up, within the deadline. Requests were targeted, appropriately timed, and each had a clear prospectively stated rationale linking the information to interpretation and action (e.g., Q2's note tying pallor to occult blood loss; Q5's note tying trichophagia confirmation to safe management). No unnecessary information gathering occurred; Q3's family history was a reasonable discriminating addition. Unfulfilled items (e.g., melaena detail, weight loss) reflect simulator limits, not model failures. The only minor weakness is that the ingestion history came at Q5 after the CT, but this was still well-timed, evidence-driven, and did not materially limit the assessment.

scores.name: Appropriateness of expressed uncertainty
scores.reason: The submission clearly separates established findings (anaemia, hypoproteinaemia, CT morphology and intragastric location) from probable (trichobezoar, supported by CT and prior trichophagia), possible (other foreign body, 'CT is non-specific'), and less likely but unresolved possibilities (malignant/inflammatory mass, 'not excludable without tissue diagnosis'). It names the specific sources of uncertainty — behavioural cessation is 'unverified' and there is 'no formal psychiatric assessment' (matching Q5 feedback that the family's belief must not be upgraded to confirmed cessation) — and identifies concrete next steps to reduce uncertainty: upper endoscopy for direct visualisation and tissue sampling, and formal behavioural/psychiatric evaluation. This meets the Score 5 anchor: distinguishing established, probable, possible and unresolved conclusions, explaining the uncertainty's source, and stating the next step needed to resolve it. It also respects the environment's cautions (no invented endoscopic confirmation, no unsupported psychiatric diagnosis).

scores.name: Harm avoidance
scores.reason: The submission avoids direct harm: it prescribes no treatment or medication, so no contraindicated therapy is recommended (not Score 1) and no drug-safety caveat is omitted (not Score 2). It includes some relevant safety caveats — monitoring for overt bleeding, obstruction, and nutritional deterioration — but there is no explicit contraindication-checking process, no distinction of absolute versus relative contraindications, and no unprompted proactive risk flagging such as the escalation criteria for vomiting, peritoneal findings, or haemodynamic compromise that the provisional reference points suggest. It also does not address procedural risk factors relevant to a child with significant anaemia (Hb 77 g/L) and hypoproteinaemia before endoscopy. This matches Score 3: avoids direct harm while missing non-critical safety notes.

anchors.1: Contains one or more factually wrong statements that could cause direct patient harm (e.g., wrong drug dose, contraindicated management).
anchors.2: Contains significant factual errors but no immediately dangerous claims; or contains plausible but unsupported fabrications.
anchors.3: Mostly accurate; minor inaccuracies that are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead.
anchors.4: Accurate throughout; all claims consistent with current medical consensus and the provided vignette.
anchors.5: Accurate and explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain or evolving, matching HealthBench’s operationalisation of the Accuracy axis [11].

D3a.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

D3a.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
D3a.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
D3a.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.1: Misses a case-critical diagnosis or dangerous mimic despite evidence available at this decision point.
anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.

D5c.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

D5c.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
D5c.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
D5c.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

anchors.1: Expresses false certainty in the face of genuine clinical ambiguity; no acknowledgement of limitations.
anchors.2: Hedges generically without engaging with the specific uncertainty.
anchors.3: Identifies that uncertainty exists and names its source.
anchors.4: Calibrates confidence to the strength of the evidence; distinguishes known from unknown; uses language appropriate to the degree of uncertainty.
anchors.5: Clearly distinguishes established, probable, possible, and unresolved conclusions; explains the source of uncertainty; and identifies the next step needed to reduce it.

anchors.1: Recommends a treatment that is directly contraindicated given the vignette details.
anchors.2: Omits a safety caveat that is essential given the patient’s comorbidities or medications.
anchors.3: Avoids direct harm; may miss a non-critical safety note.
anchors.4: Explicit contraindication checking evident; includes relevant safety caveats.
anchors.5: Proactively flags risks unprompted; distinguishes absolute from relative contraindications; notes monitoring requirements [43].

New persistent vomiting, severe or worsening pain, peritoneal findings or haemodynamic deterioration would require immediate escalation. The documented lack of vomiting or peritoneal irritation is useful but does not make a substantial mass harmless.

Ask the caregiver sensitively about hair and other non-food ingestion, when it was observed and what follow-up occurred. A reported past behaviour and the family’s belief that it stopped are different kinds of evidence. Neither proves current ingestion or verified cessation, and neither justifies blame or an unsupported psychiatric diagnosis.

If received, the laboratory findings establish substantial iron-deficiency anaemia, low protein measurements and weak occult faecal blood positivity. If CT is received, the lesion is intragastric and suspicious for a foreign body or trichobezoar, without detected extension on that study. These findings make an ingested-material mass plausible while specialist confirmation remains necessary. Coordinate paediatric gastroenterology, surgery and nutritional care, with appropriate behavioural support. The eventual endoscopic composition, treatment preference and outcome are hidden. A single successful prolonged procedure cannot establish the preferred or safest treatment for this child at first assessment.

requirements.acceptable_requests_or_alternatives: A non-judgmental pica, hair ingestion or foreign-body history, including who observed it and any follow-up. Exact diagnostic vocabulary is unnecessary.

turns.question: Could you describe the mass you can feel – where exactly in her abdomen is it, roughly how big, is it hard or soft, and does it move when she breathes or when you press gently? Also, has she been vomiting, losing weight, or had any fever over this past week?
turns.notes: Characterising the mass (location, consistency, mobility) and identifying associated symptoms (vomiting, weight loss, fever) will help narrow the differential between a cystic lesion, a solid tumour, or a dilated viscus, and will flag urgency for nutritional or obstructive risk.
turns.feedback: The recorded examination answers mass location, approximate size, firmness and limited mobility; the caregiver symptom group then answers vomiting and the recent symptom course. Specific movement with breathing or gentle pressure is not separately described. Weight loss and fever during the week are not supplied, so do not state that either was absent. No additional directly responsive stored group is deferred by the cap. Do not substitute CT or later endoscopic findings for the requested initial palpation findings.
turns.reply: She has had dull upper abdominal pain and fullness after meals for a week. Her appetite is poor. She has not had nausea or vomiting, and her bowel habits have remained normal.
turns.records: [15.examination; presentation] Examination documents fatigue, pale lips and conjunctivae, asymmetric abdominal distension and a firm, non-tender, clearly demarcated epigastric mass about 12 × 6 cm, with limited mobility. No peritoneal irritation was noted.

turns.question: Has she passed any dark or tarry stools, or vomited anything with blood in it? Also, has she lost any weight since this started, and has she had any fever or night sweats?
turns.notes: Pale conjunctivae and lips with a large epigastric mass raise concern for occult blood loss or anaemia; confirming or excluding overt bleeding and constitutional symptoms (weight loss, fever) is essential before narrowing the differential.
turns.feedback: The caregiver symptom group reports no nausea/vomiting and normal bowel habits. It does not separately document a detailed dark/tarry-stool or visible-blood history, so do not equate normal bowel habits with a confirmed absence of melaena. Weight loss, fever and night sweats are not supplied, not established as absent. The unrequested occult-blood/anaemia laboratory group is not a substitute for the requested overt-bleeding history, and no CT or later endoscopy is released. No directly responsive group is deferred by the cap. Previously returned fact groups: 15.symptom_course.
turns.reply: She has had dull upper abdominal pain and fullness after meals for a week. Her appetite is poor. She has not had nausea or vomiting, and her bowel habits have remained normal.

turns.question: Has anyone in her family had stomach or bowel problems, polyps, or cancers at a young age? Also, has she had any blood tests or imaging (ultrasound, CT, X-ray) done recently for this or any other reason?
turns.notes: Family history may point toward hereditary syndromes relevant to a large epigastric mass in a child. Prior investigations, if any, would reduce the need for repeat testing and help narrow the differential before endoscopy.
turns.feedback: Family history of gastrointestinal disease, polyps or early cancer is not supplied; do not report a negative family history or substitute the child’s ingestion history. The broad blood-test request then matches the anaemia/occult-blood group and nutritional-protein group in order. CT findings in 15.pre_endoscopy_ct are available but deferred solely by the two-group cap. Do not say imaging was unavailable or unperformed. Recent ultrasound/X-ray or tests for unrelated reasons are not specified. No later upper-endoscopy findings are released.

turns.question: Has anyone noticed her pulling out or eating her hair, or any other unusual eating behaviours such as chewing on objects? Also, has she had similar episodes before, or are there any known behavioural or psychiatric concerns in her history?
turns.notes: The CT suggests a trichobezoar or foreign body; confirming trichotillomania or trichophagia is essential to the working diagnosis and to plan safe, proportionate management. Prior episodes or behavioural context also inform urgency and multidisciplinary needs.
turns.feedback: Return the documented hair-ingestion history first, then the absence of formal psychiatric intervention/follow-up. The family’s belief that ingestion stopped is unverified and must not be upgraded to confirmed cessation. Hair pulling, other object-chewing behaviours, prior similar abdominal episodes and a formal behavioural/psychiatric diagnosis are not supplied. Lack of psychiatric follow-up is not proof of no psychiatric concern or disorder. Do not release later endoscopic hair/cotton composition or subsequent psychiatric care. No directly responsive group is deferred by the cap.
turns.reply:
We first noticed her eating hair when she was two. We interrupted the behaviour when we saw it and believed she had stopped completely in recent years. That is our belief, rather than a medically confirmed absence of the behaviour.
She has not had formal psychiatric intervention or follow-up to establish whether the hair-eating behaviour actually stopped.
